chapter_theme: The guide shows the maiden the hills, rivers, elephants and women of the Vidyadhara host as it crosses the sky, after which the party lands at Podanam, and the poet lays out the camp, its elephants, chariots, palaces and the allied kings around the royal banner.

cast.role: the woman who points out the sights to the maiden, taken as her companion; named only by a feminine verb
the Vidyadhara king's daughter, addressed as 'nangai' and 'paavaai', unnamed here
the Vidyadhara king's host, in the sky and then at camp
the elephants of the hills and of the camp
the women who travel with the host
the allied kings who camp beside the host

875.reading: The poet says that, as the vast host passes through the sky over seas, great peaks and hill-top streams, she makes all of them known to the maiden, who bows to each.
875.nuance: The verse opens the tour of the land below and rests on the repeated word அமிதம், used four times; the guide is only a feminine verb here and is taken to be the maiden's companion.
875.event: The guide names to the maiden the seas, mountains and streams that the Vidyadhara host passes over in the sky.

876.reading: The guide tells the maiden to look at the golden mountain's falling Ganga and its wishing-tree groves, which seem small from the sky yet would measure the earthly world for those who dwell there.
876.nuance: The tour shows the land by setting two worlds against each other, ours and the upper one, each measured by the other.
876.event: The guide points out the heavenly river and groves to the maiden from the moving host.

877.reading: The guide describes a river whose foam is like sandal-paste and whose bees are its birds, bringing sandal logs to the bank and breaking against the eastern sea's waves without rest.
877.nuance: The poet turns the river into a person: foam as ointment, waves as hands, bees as birds. The word division of this verse is broken and several words are rare, so the sense is held loosely.

878.reading: The guide says a river called the Sindhu, born at the foot of that mountain and flowing to the right of their own hill, plays like a girl striking a ball of foam with the palms of its gold waves.
878.nuance: The only river named in the tour is the Sindhu; the sense of the last line rests on a rare word and is held loosely.

879.reading: The guide shows a river that throws up jewels from the sandal groves, runs through hills in the waves and beats against the shore like the eastern sea, never ceasing.
879.nuance: The verse repeats the closing refrain of 877 about the waves of the eastern sea. The word division of this verse is broken and several words are rare, so the sense is held loosely.

880.reading: The guide bids the maiden see the wild elephants, mixed with honey and milk, that rage at the thunder of clouds drifting over the host and take it for a rival elephant.
880.nuance: The epithet 'the elephant-like mountain' casts the clouds and the herd as rivals; the lines 2 to 3 are clipped.
880.event: The guide points to the forest elephants raging at the clouds above the host.

881.reading: The guide shows rivers coming down from the great hills, bearing the smell of rutting elephants' must, which seem to scatter a string of pearls for the maiden to see.
881.nuance: The verse is a continuing scene of the tour; the word division is broken.

882.reading: The guide describes the hills with falling streams that look like white banners raised against the host and like hands that scatter pearls and gems at the passers-by.
882.nuance: The streams are made the banners of a rival army raised before the host; the conceit makes the landscape an opponent that yields.

883.reading: The guide points to tusker pairs playing like hills, goring the hillside so that jewels pour out like chests overturned on both sides.
883.event: Pairs of elephants gore the hillside and spill gems.

884.reading: The guide describes female elephants circling a bull that sports under a hill stream, whose raised red dust looks like saffron powder over the peaks.
884.nuance: This verse and the next two are the guide's remarks to the maiden at a point where the tour turns to the host's own life.
884.event: A bull elephant plays in the stream among his herd of cows.

885.reading: The guide shows how the jewelled chariots in their ranks turn about in the ocean of the host, moving so smoothly across the clear crystal sky that the eye cannot catch their going.
885.event: The Vidyadhara chariot horses wheel in the host's ranks in the sky.

886.reading: The guide points to a young woman of the host whose loosened hair and wind-blown garlands and robe let fall her girdle, the sparkling ornaments dropping about her.
886.nuance: The poet draws the woman's unwinding dress as an unconscious show; the verse carries no reproof.
886.event: A young woman of the host loses her robe and ornaments in the wind.

887.reading: The guide shows women of the host trembling from the mist of fine drops from clouds and the must of elephants and hiding in their husbands' arms, spreading their robes from shyness before many.
887.nuance: The shyness here is playful and shown as seemly; the verse is the one in the tour that sets desire against modesty.
887.event: The women of the host hide in their lovers' chests and draw their robes against the drizzle and the crowd.

888.reading: The guide says the aerial cars of the host, moving to a song of play, come like a troop of hills, and bids the maiden look at their power under the sun's glare.
888.nuance: The last two lines turn on rare words and the sense is a guess.

889.reading: Having shown the young woman many such sights, the party crosses flooded fields and a lovely city and comes to a grove called the lord's seat, where they reach their stopping place.
889.nuance: The verse closes the tour and passes from the maiden's view to the host's camp.
889.event: After the tour the Vidyadhara party arrives at a grove beside Podanam.

890.reading: The host of the maiden's lord settles in a thick flower-grove; the bees swarming over the women's garlands spoil the honey.
890.nuance: Lines 1 and 4 are clipped and the sense is held loosely.
890.event: The Vidyadhara king's host makes camp in a flower grove.

891.reading: Bees that fed on the rut of angry elephants wheel away as if falling from the beasts' bound necks.
891.nuance: This is a pure picture of the camp's elephants.

892.reading: The rutting elephants burn against the sandal trunks they lean on, as the bees sing a slow note, like a post that blazes.
892.nuance: The last line compares the bull to a burning post and the comparison is hard to place.

893.reading: Steeds in tumult roll over saffron dust and flowers, and the rows of the great stables come with many gleaming hands spread out.
893.nuance: The sense turns on rare words.

894.reading: Chariots with banners and the king's royal lodgings are laid out in a circle at the camp, as if heaven itself had come down.
894.event: The camp's lodgings and chariots are set out in a ring.

895.reading: The camp has golden mansions, halls of diamond, gold dancing-halls and aloe-wood beds, all full of new richness.

896.reading: Silver pavilions set with coral, scented sleeping-halls and day-palaces fill the generous king's town.

897.reading: Tanks like drawn water, gardens that smell divine, small hills and jasmine bowers with sand slopes are all found in the camp.
897.nuance: The closing word என்பவே is the poet's formula for hearsay and sets the whole camp as report.

898.reading: The host surrounds the king's banner-hall and the fields beyond it, and the other kings, wearing pearl garlands, make for the outskirts of the forest.
898.nuance: The verse leaves unclear which king's flag-hall it means and where the forest lies.
898.event: The host rings the royal camp and the other kings pitch beside the forest.

links.note: Verse 875 starts the guide's naming of the lands below; 889 ends the tour at the grove where the host alights.
links.teaches: The tour is a framed journey that ends with the host's landing at Podanam, so the descriptions serve the arrival.

links.note: Kural 381 counts the army among the six limbs of a king; verse 898 shows an army encamped with allied kings rimming the forest around the royal banner.
links.teaches: The camp shows the army as a ring of allies as well as a limb, which the couplet's list of six does not show.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that makes the host a part of kingship, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any picture of an army in the field with its allies pitched around the king.

source_issues: Verses 877 to 888: the printed stanza ran into eight half-lines and was repaired to four lines; the word division stays broken in places.
Verses 875 to 888: the speaker is not named; the guide is taken from the feminine verb of 875 and the address to the maiden.
Verses 890 to 898: the verses are short metre with clipped grammar; several readings are held loosely.
